passage: In the eye-clinic waiting room, Parveen had just settled Nani into a plastic chair when Ujjwal Mamu spotted them. "Parveen! Final year, na? Placement done? What package?" "Not yet, Mamu. I'm applying." "Not yet? Farah got placed in second year. And after the job, marriage. Don't wait like your Khala did." Two women in the row turned to look. Parveen felt her face heat up, as if she were already late for something nobody had told her the time of. She took a breath. "I know you ask because you care, Mamu. I'm going at my own pace. I'll tell you when there's news." He blinked, then laughed. "Okay, okay." Nani patted her knee. By the time Nani's token was called, Parveen noticed her hands had stopped shaking.

qa.q: Where did Ujjwal Mamu spot Parveen and Nani?
qa.a: In the eye-clinic waiting room.

qa.q: What was Parveen feeling when the two women turned to look?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and rushed, as if she were already late for something nobody had told her the time of.

qa.q: What made Parveen's reply to Mamu a good choice?
qa.a: She recognised that he cared, stayed polite and named her own pace, without arguing or taking on his timetable.

qa.q: How might Ujjwal Mamu see his own questions?
qa.a: He probably sees them as normal family interest, measured against a timetable he believes in, so he may not realise they sting.

grounding: A young woman is quizzed by a relative about placement and marriage, feels judged and rushed, and answers kindly while keeping her own pace.

passage:
Dear Uday,
Since you're coming to the family wedding next month, let me tell you what I learnt at Diwali. Within ten minutes, three aunties asked me: job? salary? marriage? One said, "At your age I had a baby." I smiled, went up to the terrace and felt like a failed exam paper.
For a week I was angry. Then I started to see it: they're using a clock from their own time. Graduate at 21, job at 22, married at 24. It isn't my clock, but it isn't cruel either.
So here's what I say now, kindly: "I'm working on it, Aunty. How's your knee?" Short, warm, then a new subject. I don't argue and I don't promise dates.
You'll get the same questions. You don't owe anyone your timeline.
Your didi,
Pallavi

qa.q: What did one aunty say to Pallavi at Diwali?
qa.a: "At your age I had a baby."

qa.q: How did Pallavi feel on the terrace?
qa.a: Judged and small, like a failed exam paper.

qa.q: Why does Pallavi's line "I'm working on it, Aunty. How's your knee?" work?
qa.a: It is short and warm, doesn't argue or promise dates, and turns the talk to the aunty, so Pallavi stays kind without taking on their clock.

qa.q: How might the aunties see their own questions?
qa.a: They are likely following the clock of their own time and may think of the questions as ordinary interest, not judgment.

grounding: A young woman quizzed by relatives about job, salary and marriage feels judged, then learns to answer warmly without adopting their timetable.

passage: Samir, you won't believe my train journey. Twelve hours in the same compartment as Chacha. First hour: "Kunal, what's your salary?" I told him the truth. It's small; it's my first job, at the NGO. He made the face. Second hour: "A grown man in our family should earn double by now." By Jhansi it was marriage: "Your cousin's wedding is in December. Who's next?" I wanted to jump off at a station, yaar. I felt like I was running a race nobody told me I'd entered. But around Bhopal I just changed my tone. I said, "Chacha, I know you worry because you love me. I'm not behind. I'm on a different route. How did you choose your job?" He talked for an hour about his first posting and didn't ask me anything for the rest of the trip. Honestly? I liked hearing it.

qa.q: Where does Kunal work in his first job?
qa.a: At the NGO.

qa.q: How did Kunal feel by the time Chacha brought up marriage?
qa.a: He felt pressured and judged, like running a race nobody told him he'd entered.

qa.q: What turning point around Bhopal changed the journey?
qa.a: Kunal answered kindly, said he was on a different route and asked Chacha about his own job, turning pressure into a real conversation.

qa.q: What might Chacha have enjoyed about being asked how he chose his job?
qa.a: He got to share his own story and feel listened to, which may have eased his worry about Kunal.

grounding: A young man questioned about salary and marriage on a long train journey feels rushed, then answers kindly without adopting his uncle's timetable.

passage:
I'm Damini, Devika's cousin, and I was holding the new baby at my brother's naming ceremony when it started. Devika, twenty-two, had just finished her first week as a lab assistant. Within minutes three relatives had found her. Mausi: "Next it's your wedding, na? Twenty-two is the right age." Chachaji: "Lab assistant? What's the salary? Your cousin in Pune gets double." An aunty: "Don't wait too long, beta."
I can't say what was going on in her head. I saw her fingers twist the end of her dupatta and her smile go stiff. Then she took a breath and said, "When it's right for me, Mausi, you'll be the first to know. And the lab work is exactly what I wanted." She said it gently and didn't argue. Afterwards she came and took the baby from me and held it for a long time.

qa.q: What had Devika just finished?
qa.a: Her first week as a lab assistant.

qa.q: What do Devika's twisting fingers and stiff smile suggest?
qa.a: They suggest she felt uncomfortable and pressured, judged and rushed by the questions, though Damini can't be sure what she felt.

qa.q: What choice did Devika make at the turning point with Mausi?
qa.a: Instead of arguing or giving in, she said gently that she would share news when it's right for her and that she chose the lab work.

qa.q: How might Mausi see the questions compared with how Devika felt them?
qa.a: Mausi may think she is showing care by following the usual timetable, not realising the questions felt like pressure.

grounding: A cousin watches a young woman questioned about marriage and salary by relatives with a fixed timetable, who feels the pressure and answers kindly on her own terms.

passage:
Monday. Seema Pishi phoned Anirban, twenty-one, from Kolkata. "Final year done? What job? What salary? Your father had a government post at your age." When he said he had taken a two-year rural teaching fellowship, she sighed so loudly he held the phone away. He spent the evening feeling like a train that had missed its station.
Thursday. Walking back from the library, he rehearsed answers. Angry ones first. Then he tried a kinder one out loud, and a passing cyclist stared.
Sunday. At lunch in Pishi's house, she started again. "And marriage? Your cousin is engaged." Anirban put more fish on her plate. "Pishi, I love that you worry about me. I'm doing the fellowship first; the rest will come when it's right for me." She clicked her tongue, then asked what the village school was like. He told her for twenty minutes.

qa.q: What did Anirban take up instead of a regular job?
qa.a: A two-year rural teaching fellowship.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel after Monday's call?
qa.a: He felt judged and discouraged, like a train that had missed its station.

qa.q: What made Anirban's Sunday answer work better than his angry rehearsals would have?
qa.a: It thanked Pishi for caring while calmly keeping his own timeline, so she softened and asked about the school.

qa.q: Why might Seema Pishi click her tongue and then ask about the village school?
qa.a: She still measures life by the old timetable, but his warm answer let her curiosity and care show through.

grounding: Over a week a young man pressed by his aunt about job, salary and marriage feels rushed, then learns to answer kindly without taking on her clock.
